summary: Defines a framework for a protocol that lets telepresence systems interoperate. The protocol describes multiple media streams so a sender and a receiver can make sensible decisions about what to transmit, select and render. This is the framework for the CLUE work, and it is standards-track.

eli5.summary: A fancy video room might have several cameras and screens. This document sets out the big picture for how two such rooms can describe what they have, so each knows what to show and what to send.

questions: how do telepresence systems handle multiple streams
what is a media capture in clue
how does a clue consumer choose streams
what is an mcc in clue
subtitle: How telepresence rooms with many cameras and screens describe what they can send and ask for what they want.

tldr.problem: Telepresence systems have several cameras, microphones and screens, but there was no standard, cross-vendor way to describe and negotiate multiple audio and video streams, so systems from different makers could not easily interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: A Media Provider sends an Advertisement describing its Media Captures, Capture Scenes, spatial layout and encoding limits, and the Media Consumer answers with a Configure message naming the streams it wants. A normal SIP and SDP offer/answer exchange then sets up the media.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8845 is the Standards Track framework for the CLUE work, with companion documents for signaling, the data model and the protocol. It defines concepts and rules, not the wire syntax.

today: RFC 8845 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2021. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it works alongside the CLUE companion documents RFC 8846, RFC 8847, RFC 8848 and RFC 8849.

sections.title: Why Telepresence Needs a Framework
sections.content:
Telepresence systems already build on open standards such as RTP (RFC 3550) and SIP (RFC 3261), yet they cannot easily interoperate. A major cause named in the text is the lack of a standardized way to describe and negotiate the use of multiple audio and video streams.

This document is the framework for a protocol called CLUE (ControLling mUltiple streams for tElepresence). It is meant to support the use cases of RFC 7205 and meet the requirements of RFC 7262, including cases with several media streams that are not strictly telepresence. Basic session setup still uses SIP and SDP offer/answer (RFC 3264); CLUE adds signaling to exchange information about the streams. Companion documents cover the signaling (RFC 8848), the data model (RFC 8846) and the protocol (RFC 8847).

The motivations listed include: many cameras and screens with no cross-vendor way to associate them in space and time, devices that cannot be used in two setups at once (a camera zoomed to two seats cannot also show all seats), limited encoding resources, and the need to narrow the options a SIP offer/answer has to consider.
sections.eli5: Imagine two clubhouses, each with lots of cameras and TVs, built by different companies. They had no shared way to say which camera shows what. This framework is that shared way.

sections.title: Advertisement and Configure
sections.content:
The model has two roles. A Media Provider sends media; a Media Consumer receives it. An endpoint or a Multipoint Control Unit (MCU) usually plays both roles at once. The Provider describes what it can send in an Advertisement, and the Consumer replies with a Configure message saying which content and streams it wants. The Provider then sends the requested streams.

The flow starts with an ordinary SIP INVITE and SDP offer/answer that sets up a basic media session and negotiates a CLUE channel. Once that channel is established, each side sends an Advertisement and a Configure, and then a re-INVITE with updated SDP sets up the media. Advertisement and Configure typically happen at call start but MAY happen at any time. Some changes, such as asking for a different capture source, should not need heavy SIP re-invites, while others, such as moving from one screen to several with more bandwidth, do need a new offer/answer.

A CLUE-capable device can interoperate with one that does not support CLUE. It learns from the first offer/answer whether the other side wants CLUE, and if not it falls back to behavior that does not require it. The renderer inside a Consumer is not specified; it may ignore some of the Provider's information.
sections.eli5: One room says, here is everything I can show you. The other room answers, I would like these three, please. Only then do they start sending video.

sections.title: Spatial Relationships
sections.content:
To render streams sensibly, a Consumer often needs to know where captures sit relative to each other. CLUE defines a coordinate system for this. Each Capture Scene has its own coordinate system, unrelated to those of other scenes. The system is right-handed Cartesian X, Y, Z, with the origin wherever the Provider chooses, and the Provider MUST use the same system, scale and origin for everything in one scene.

Coordinates come in three scales. Millimeters means real physical units, and systems that know their physical dimensions MUST provide them. Unknown Scale means the scale is not necessarily millimeters but is the same for every capture in the scene, and systems that know only relative distances MUST use it. No Scale means the scale may differ per capture; it is intended for cases such as an MCU forwarding captures from different endpoints side by side.

X increases from left to right as seen by an observer at the front of the room looking toward the back, Y increases from front to back, and Z increases from floor to ceiling.
sections.eli5: It is like drawing a map of the room with a left-right line, a front-back line and an up-down line, so everyone agrees where each camera is pointing.

sections.title: Media Captures, Scenes and MCCs
sections.content:
A Media Capture is the basic unit a device can send. It can be the output of a camera or microphone, a laptop or DVD player, an audio mixer or video composer, or a concept such as 'the loudest speaker'. A capture is of a single media type, has a unique identity such as VC1 or AC1, has exactly one set of spatial information, and can be the source of at most one Capture Encoding. All attributes are optional. They include Point of Capture, Point on Line of Capture, Area of Capture (four co-planar points, video only), Mobility of Capture (static, dynamic, highly dynamic), Audio Capture Sensitivity Pattern, Description, Presentation, View (Room, Table, Individual, Lectern, Audience), Language, Person Information (xCard), Person Type, Priority, Embedded Text and Related To.

A Capture Scene is a spatial region, such as a room, that groups captures. Inside it, Capture Scene Views (CSVs) are lists of captures of one media type that together are one way to represent the scene. The Provider MUST be able to send all captures in a single CSV at once. Different CSVs are alternatives the Provider suggests, such as three cameras covering the room versus one camera showing the center. An optional Global View List suggests sets of CSVs across all scenes.

A Multiple Content Capture (MCC) mixes or switches other captures of one type. Its MaxCaptures attribute sets how many may appear in the encoding at a time, which separates switched, composed and switched-and-composed cases. A Policy attribute such as SoundLevel or RoundRobin says how content is chosen, a SynchronizationID keeps several MCCs showing the same source, and Allow Subset Choice lets the Consumer pick a subset of the referenced captures.
sections.eli5: A capture is one camera or microphone feed, with a name tag. A scene is a room with all its feeds, and an MCC is a feed that flips between others, like a director cutting to whoever is talking.

sections.title: Simultaneity and Encoding Limits
sections.content:
A Provider may be unable to send some captures together. A Simultaneous Transmission Set lists captures of one media type that can be sent at the same time. In the RFC's example, three cameras give VC0, VC1 and VC2, and the middle camera can also zoom out to show all six people as VC3. It cannot do both, so the sets are {VC0, VC1, VC2} and {VC0, VC3, VC2}, and the Consumer MUST choose captures wholly within one set.

The second kind of limit is encoding resources. An Individual Encoding is a way to encode a capture; its parameters (such as maximum bandwidth, picture size and pixels per second for H.26x video) live in SDP, not in CLUE messages. An Encoding Group bundles Individual Encodings and a maximum bitrate for all of them combined. Each capture encoding MUST stay within its Individual Encoding's maximum, and the sum MUST stay within the group's value. A capture MUST be associated with an Encoding Group to be eligible for configuration.
sections.eli5: A camera cannot zoom in and zoom out at the same moment, and a room only has so much internet to share. These rules let a room say, you can have this or that, but not both, and not more than this much in total.

sections.title: How a Consumer Chooses Streams
sections.content:
After receiving an Advertisement, the Consumer builds a Configure message, a list of Capture Encodings where each one names one Media Capture and one Individual Encoding from that capture's Encoding Group. The Consumer is free to use the Advertisement as it likes, but three considerations are called out: local preference (an endpoint tends to pick captures that match its number of displays, an MCU may prefer loudest-speaker streams over pre-composed video), the Provider's physical simultaneity limits, and encoding and Encoding Group limits. On the last point the Consumer MUST ensure each requested stream fits its Encoding and the combined streams fit their Encoding Groups.

For an MCC listed as MCC1(VC1,VC2,VC3), a Consumer that does not want VC3 can return MCC1(VC1,VC2), but only if Allow Subset Choice is true. The Consumer needs at least one Advertisement and an SDP offer defining the Individual Encodings before its first Configure, and it can send a new Configure at any time, valid against the most recent Advertisement. Encodings sent over RTP must conform to the most recent SDP offer/answer result.
sections.eli5: The receiving room looks at the menu, picks the dishes that fit its number of plates and appetite, and tells the sender exactly how to cook each one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The text notes several possible attacks: an endpoint listening to sessions it is not authorized to join, trying to disconnect or mute others, or stealing service by creating sessions it is not allowed to. MCUs are advised to follow conference control security recommendations, and the security considerations in RFC 4579 MUST be followed.

CLUE uses SIP and SDP to establish the session before any CLUE information is exchanged, so SIP security, including user authentication and authorization, MUST be supported. Media MUST be secured: DTLS/SRTP MUST be supported and SHOULD be used unless the RTP media is secured by other means. Privacy is a concern for xCard data and the free-text description fields, which could reveal sensitive information, so an implementation SHOULD give users control over what is sent in an Advertisement. Because xCard and description content is not guaranteed authentic, it MUST NOT be used for authorization decisions.
sections.eli5: Before you show people your room, you check who is calling. You should also be careful what you put on your name tags, because anyone can write anything on a name tag.
